text:
Quentin had a way of arriving at parties that suggested the party had been organized in anticipation of him. Not late, because late was a strategy for the merely famous. Not early, because early was for people who wanted to be thanked. He arrived at the exact minute the host would have wished for, with a gift that seemed to have been chosen by a committee of people who knew the host personally, and then he spent the evening being useful to everyone except himself. I met him in my sophomore year, in a seminar on the history of American cities, in a building that smelled of radiator dust and ambition. There were eleven of us. I remember this because the professor counted us aloud on the first day, the way you confirm the presence of livestock, and because I had spent the entire previous semester in courses of two hundred where I was a number with a face.

He was called Quentin. Everyone called him Q, though I suspect he had never asked anyone to. It happened the way things happened around him, effortlessly, as though the shorter version were simply the honest one. He had a long, narrow face, very straight eyebrows, and a habit of standing with his arms crossed that made him look like a man reviewing evidence. He wrote his notes in blue ink, in a small, immaculate hand, and he never once used the phrase "I guess." I became aware of this the way you become aware of a missing sound: by noticing its absence in everyone else.

By the second semester I was taking the seminar not for the credit but to sit near him, which I have never admitted to anyone, including myself, until this year, when I watched him do something at a public swimming pool that made me want to drive home and sit on my kitchen floor for a while.

Here is what I mean by flawless, because I have spent ten years trying to be precise about it. Q never lost an argument he could have won, and I mean never, not once, not even in the friendly, losing-for-sport way that most people allow themselves at least monthly. He did not get sick. He did not have a phase. He graduated with honors in something I can no longer remember, which is its own small indictment of my own career, and then he went to work at a firm whose name he never had to say out loud, because it was the sort of name that made people straighten up when they heard it. Women at parties seemed to orbit him the way the seminar students orbited the professor. He was the sort of person who could make a waiter feel that the mistake had been the waiter's.

And I was the sort of person who was not that. I was, in fact, the person at the table who said "I guess" constantly, who got the flu every winter like a scheduled appointment, who once argued about the merits of a restaurant and lost so badly that I went to my car and cried in a way I found undignified even then. I liked him anyway. I liked him the way you like a lighthouse, which is to say from a distance, and with some resentment that he was so much taller than you.

We drifted apart the way college friendships do, which is to say slowly, and then all at once, and then with a kind of embarrassed relief, as though we had both been carrying a thing we didn't want to keep carrying. He got a job that involved moving, and I got a job that involved staying, and the two of us exchanged texts at a frequency that I now understand was a mutual act of mercy. He wrote to me once, a long message, very well composed, about something I can't remember, and I wrote back three sentences, and he did not write back again, and we let that be the end of it, which was, in its way, very much like Q.

This is the version of the story I would have told you a year ago. Q, the flawless one, out there somewhere, presumably flawless still, presumably making some other young person at some other party feel exactly the way I felt in that seminar: useful, seen, slightly ashamed of the gap.

Then I went to a wedding in a town in New Jersey where the heat was the kind that makes asphalt feel personal, and on the second day I needed, badly, to be in water.

The municipal pool was the sort of place that exists to be a little embarrassing, a low concrete basin under a canvas roof, with a snack bar that sold pretzels and ice cream from a machine that looked like a piece of farm equipment. There was a lifeguard in a tall chair with a whistle she blew at intervals, not at anything in particular. There was a man doing what I can only describe as a meditation on the deep end, floating on his back with his eyes closed, arms out, like a very calm dead person. And there, at a table beneath a striped umbrella near the snack bar, were two people with drinks, and one of them was Q.

I want to be careful about the moment of recognition, because I have a reputation among my own thoughts for dramatizing things. It was not dramatic. It was the opposite of dramatic. He was wearing a white polo shirt and shorts and sunglasses that sat on his head like a hat, and he was holding his paper cup with both hands, and the sunlight was doing something unflattering to his jaw that I had never seen, because I had never seen him unflattering, ever, and there it was, on his face, like weather.

He had a woman with him. I never learned her name. She was maybe his age, with wet hair pulled back and a towel over her shoulder, and she was talking, and he was doing the thing he did when he was thinking about what to say, which was to listen with perfect attention, nodding at exactly the right intervals, his face arranged into an expression of engaged consideration that I recognized the way a dog recognizes a whistle.

She was talking about the summer, about the apartment, about how the heat had gotten to her mother's garden, about a promotion she had been hoping for that had gone to someone else. She was doing the thing people do when they need to be told something by someone they love and they are not yet ready to say it themselves, which is to fill the silence with everything else.

And then he did something I will not soon forget. He said, "Okay," in a voice pitched for an audience, and he said, "I want to talk to you about my situation at work," and she stopped talking, and the lifeguard blew her whistle at something off in the deep end, and I understood that we were all, now, in on it.

He had come to this pool to tell her he had been let go. I did not know that yet. I am telling you what I understood afterward, which is what I understood as it happened, in pieces, like a sentence assembled out of its parts.

He explained that the firm had undergone "a restructuring." He explained that the word "fired" was, in his view, "a loaded term that doesn't do justice to the complexity of what happened." He explained that there were "many factors," and that he had been thinking about it "from a number of angles," and that the honest summary was that it was a "mutual realignment of expectations," which he said, and I am not exaggerating, with a little smile, as though he had just invented it and wanted credit.

She said, "Quentin, did you get fired?"

He said, "I wouldn't frame it that way."

She said, "Did you get fired?"

He said, "I'd rather say I was part of a reduction."

There was a silence then, and the snack bar woman came out and asked them if they wanted more ice cream, and neither of them answered, and she looked between them the way people do when two humans at a table have gone strange, and went back in.

What I watched next was the most interesting thing I have seen in a long time, and I need you to understand that I did not enjoy it in any simple way. It was like watching someone play a piano they had practiced all their life, badly. Q kept going. He explained that the severance package was actually "quite robust." He explained that he had been planning, for some time, for "a pivot," and that this was, from a distance, almost an opportunity. He used the word "pivot" three times. He used the word "actually" five. He told her that the important thing was that he had never felt "more clear about what I want to do next," and he said this while looking at the water, at the meditating man, at anything except the woman sitting across from him who was, by this point, not crying, because she was better than that, but holding her cup in both hands the way he held his, as though steadying herself against something.

"Can you just tell me what happened," she said. "In one sentence. Like you're telling your mother."

And here is where I had to look away, because I knew the sentence. I had known it since he said "restructuring," because I had spent a decade knowing that man, and the sentence was the one thing he could not make smooth. He opened his mouth. He said, "Well, the way I'm seeing it, and I want to be careful, because I don't want you to hear this as, there was a disagreement between me and the managing partner about the direction of the practice, and it became untenable, and so we went our separate ways, and I want to be clear that it wasn't a character judgment, it was a, there are different philosophies about how a firm like that should, and I think mine was actually the better one, historically, but it wasn't aligned with what they were looking for, and so, and I know that sounds complicated, and I don't want you to think I'm, you know, making excuses. I'm just telling you what happened."

He had talked for a full minute without a comma. She listened to all of it. Then she put her cup down, very gently, the way you put down a glass of water you no longer want, and she said, "You got fired."

"I got let go," he said, but without any of the earlier conviction, and the distinction between the two phrases, which had been his entire architecture, stood there in the poolside air like a little ruined shed.

She stood up. She said, "I'm going to get out of the water," and then, after a pause, "I'm going to get out of the water and we can talk about this when you've had time to think about whether 'restructuring' was the right word for it," and I realized, watching her walk toward the changing area with her towel over her shoulder, that she was not leaving him. She was giving him the same thing he had given her, which was a framework, a structure, a way to walk around the word. She was doing the thing he was so good at, and she had learned it from him, and she was using it on him, and it was the most Q-like thing I had ever seen anyone do.

He sat there for a while with his two paper cups. He picked up one and drank from it, and then set it down, and picked up the other, and set it down, and I watched him take off his sunglasses and put them back on again, which is a small gesture, and I have never seen him make a small gesture.

I want to tell you that I was moved. I want to tell you that I sat there feeling a swell of something, brotherhood, solidarity, the human recognition of one flawed creature in another. I was moved, yes, but it was a complicated moving, the way a house moves in an earthquake, which is to say in all directions at once, and mostly downward. Because here was the thing I had never been able to say out loud, not to him, not to my friends, not even, until now, to myself: I had spent ten years believing that the gap between us was a fact about the world, a fixed geography. He was the man with the blue ink and the straight eyebrows, and I was the man who cried in his car about restaurants, and the distance between those two things was the distance between a lighthouse and a beach, permanent and structural, something you accepted the way you accept weather.

But watching him sit there with his two cups, I understood that the flawlessness was not a fact about him either. It was a technique. It was the same thing I did when I said "I guess" a hundred times, only done better, only done with more confidence and more blue ink. He couldn't be casual. He couldn't be sloppy, or unfinished, or wrong in front of someone he cared about, because those states had been trained out of him somewhere, or trained into him, and now they had come home to roost at a municipal pool in New Jersey, in the middle of a woman's ruined summer, over ice cream from a farm machine.

He had a difficulty. Not a secret, not a darkness, not the kind of difficulty that would have made a good story about me discovering the hidden wound beneath the armor. A difficulty like mine. A difficulty like the one I had in my kitchen last winter, when I couldn't tell my mother that I was unhappy, because telling her would have required saying it plainly, and I am, and this was always true, just a worse version of the same animal as Quentin: an animal that cannot survive being seen mid-sentence.

I left before he finished his second cup. I walked out through the snack bar, past the pretzel display, and into the heat, and I did not look back, because I understood, finally, what looking back would have meant. It would have meant being recognized. It would have meant the seminar again, the counting of heads, the eleven of us, and him standing with his arms crossed, reviewing the evidence of my ten years of ordinary life, and me standing there, unflattering in the sun, unable to explain myself in one sentence.

He would have been kind. I know he would have been kind, because I know now that he is kind, the way he was kind when he gave me the long, well-composed text and then never wrote again, which was kindness done his way, with structure, with care for the shape of things. He would have said something about the reunion, something with the word "robust" in it, and we would have had a beautiful conversation about old times, and I would have gone home having learned nothing.

Instead I drove home with the windows down, and I sat on my kitchen floor for a while, which I have found, over the years, to be my own version of floating on my back in the deep end, arms out, eyes closed. And then I got up, and I opened my laptop, and I wrote a text to Quentin that was three sentences long, the same length as my last one, the last of the last ones, ten years ago, and it said, roughly, that I had seen him at a pool, that he seemed like he was having a rough summer, and that I was sorry I hadn't called sooner.

I have not heard back. Or perhaps he has, and put it in his inbox, and will address it when he has finished thinking about it from a number of angles, which I understand, now, is not the same as never. It is just slower. It is just done in blue ink.
